sum(n_expected, na.rm = TRUE),       n_expected     ),     rate_observed = case_when(       is.na(interval_length) & n_enrolled == 0 ~ 0,       is.na(interval_length) ~ n_enrolled / tail_length_piece,       TRUE ~ n_enrolled / interval_length     )   ) %>%   select(     enroll_interval,     n_enrolled,     n_expected,     rate_observed,     rate_expected   )  enroll_curve_piece <- dat_piece %>%   arrange(enrollTime) %>%   mutate(cumulative_n = row_number()) interval_summary_piece %>%   knitr::kable(     caption = "Observed enrollment by calendar interval"   ) ggplot2::ggplot(dat_piece, aes(x = enrollTime)) +   geom_histogram(     binwidth = 2,     boundary = 0,     fill = "steelblue",     alpha = 0.35,     color = "black",     linewidth = 0.3   ) +   geom_vline(     xintercept = cutpoints_piece[-c(1, length(cutpoints_piece))],     linetype = "dashed",     color = "firebrick"   ) +   labs(     x = "Enrollment time",     y = "Number enrolled",     title = "Piecewise Poisson-process enrollment"   ) +   theme_bw() ggplot2::ggplot(enroll_curve_piece, aes(x = enrollTime, y = cumulative_n)) +   geom_step(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_vline(     xintercept = cutpoints_piece[-c(1, length(cutpoints_piece))],     linetype = "dashed",     color = "firebrick"   ) +   labs(     x = "Enrollment time",     y = "Cumulative number enrolled",     title = "Cumulative enrollment under piecewise accrual"   ) +   theme_bw()

text: Suppose want simulate longitudinal continuous outcome measured fixed set visits, trajectories differ treatment group. illustration, consider marginal mean model \[ Y_{t}=\beta_0+\beta_{\text {time }} t+\beta_{\text {trt }} x_i+\beta_{\text {time:trt }} t x_i+\varepsilon_{t}, \quad =1, \ldots, n, \quad t \\{0,1, \ldots, T-1\}, \] \(x_i \\{0,1\}\) treatment indicator residual vector \(\varepsilon_i=\left(\varepsilon_{0}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{, T-1}\right)^{\top}\) follows \[ e_i \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{V}\right), \quad \mathbf{V}_{t t^{\prime}}=\rho^{\left|t-t^{\prime}\right|} \] \(\mathbf{V}\) standard AR(1) correlation structure: measurements closer time strongly correlated. explicitly, can written \[\mathbf{V}=\left(\begin{array}{ccccc}1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \cdots & \rho^{n-1} \\ \rho & 1 & \rho & \cdots & \rho^{n-2} \\ \rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \cdots & \rho^{n-3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \rho^{n-1} & \rho^{n-2} & \rho^{n-3} & \cdots & 1\end{array}\right)\] example use: \(\mathrm{AR}(1)\) correlation \(\rho=0.5\), \(T=5\) visits (baseline + 4 follow-visits), constant control-group mean time, non-linear treatment effect across visits, residual SD \(\sigma=0.95\). Step 1: Specify within-subject correlation encode AR(1) structure directly using corr_make(): Step 2: Treat visit “correlated endpoint” Although endpoint_details typically describes distinct endpoints, can also use represent distinct visits single longitudinal outcome. entry specifies marginal mean visit control, plus visit-specific treatment effect. Step 3: Simulate wide data makeData() Wide data returned makeData() (one column per visit) stage standard “wide” format dataset: visit appears separate column (Cont_1, …, Cont_5). key observation collection correlated endpoints can interpreted repeated measures reshape data. Step 4: Convert wide \(\rightarrow\) long long data now looks like typical longitudinal dataset: Longitudinal data reshaping long format Step 5: Validate intended effects correlation verify simulated data reflect intended mean structure AR(1) correlation, fit marginal model using geeM::geem(): Inspecting output model, observe simulation proceeded correctly: True vs. estimated longitudinal treatment effects correlation parameters. (Note: \(\sigma\) marginal residual SD \(\varepsilon_{} \sim N(0,\sigma^2\mathbf{V})\)) now longitudinal data set correct data characteristics use simulation. Finally, can visualize small set subject trajectories:

constant residual error  baseline <- list(   endpoint_type = "continuous",   baseline_mean = 0.45,   trt_effect    = 0,     # no baseline difference   sd            = sigma )  v1 <- list(endpoint_type = "continuous", baseline_mean = 0.45, trt_effect = -0.10, sd = sigma) v2 <- list(endpoint_type = "continuous", baseline_mean = 0.45, trt_effect = -0.15, sd = sigma) v3 <- list(endpoint_type = "continuous", baseline_mean = 0.45, trt_effect = -0.25, sd = sigma) v4 <- list(endpoint_type = "continuous", baseline_mean = 0.45, trt_effect = -0.40, sd = sigma) correlated_visits_wide <- makeData(   correlation_matrix    = corMat_5_visits,   SEED                  = 321,   sample_size_per_group = 2000,   # text: alternative way generate longitudinal data using endpoints framework simulate subject-specific random effects use latent quantities inside separate longitudinal data-generating process. approach often natural longitudinal outcome intended follow mixed-effects model, directly represents patient-level heterogeneity random intercepts slopes. example, consider following longitudinal model random intercept random slope: \[ \begin{gathered} y_{ijt} = \underbrace{(\beta_0 + \beta_1 j + \alpha_i)}_{\text{intercepts}} + t\,\underbrace{(\beta_2 + \beta_{1:2} j + \gamma_i)}_{\text{slopes}} + \epsilon_{ijt} \\ \epsilon_{ijt} \sim N(0,\sigma^2) \quad \text{} \quad \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_i \\ \gamma_i \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N} \!\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \mathbf{\Lambda} \right) \quad \text{} \quad\mathbf{\Lambda} = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_\alpha^2 & \rho_{\alpha\gamma}\sigma_\alpha\sigma_\gamma \\ \rho_{\alpha\gamma}\sigma_\alpha\sigma_\gamma & \sigma_\gamma^2 \end{pmatrix}. \end{gathered} \] : - \(j \\{0,1\}\) indicates treatment group ( \(0=\) control, \(1=\) treatment), - \(\) indexes subjects, - \(t\) indexes time, - \(\alpha_i\) subject-specific random intercept, - \(\gamma_i\) subject-specific random slope. formulation, correlation repeated measurements induced shared random effects rather directly specifying within-subject correlation matrix across visits. Two-stage Simulation Strategy basic idea proceed two steps: Use makeData() simulate subject-level latent variables (e.g., random intercepts, random slopes, additional endpoints TTE outcomes). Use subject-level quantities inside second helper function expands data time generates repeated measurements. approach especially useful longitudinal outcome must correlated endpoints (e.g., hospitalization mortality), since makeData() can generate latent subject-level quantities jointly. Example: Random Effects & Two TTE Endpoints example simulate trial : one fatal TTE endpoint: -cause mortality (ACM), one non-fatal TTE endpoint: hospitalization (HP), one latent random intercept, one latent random slope. first define correlation matrix, encodes dependence among four subject-level quantities: Next, specify two random effects continuous endpoints centered 0: define two TTE endpoints: Now use makeData() generate subject-level dataset, subject latent random effects generated. example, cap subject-level follow-4 time units: stage, simulated dataset contains: TTE_1: -cause mortality, TTE_2: hospitalization, Cont_1: random intercept, Cont_2: random slope. subject-level quantities. remaining step expand data time generate repeated longitudinal measurements. Creating Longitudinal Data , use small helper function : expands subject across time grid, evaluates user-supplied linear predictor, adds Gaussian residual error, optionally censors longitudinal outcome fatal event. example , linear predictor includes: fixed intercept 10, baseline treatment effect, control-group slope \(-\mathbf{0 . 5}\), treatment--time interaction +1 , subject-specific random intercept ( Cont_1 ), subject-specific random slope ( Cont_2 * time ). first generate latent longitudinal outcome without censoring, can verify fixed random effects separately TTE censoring mechanism. Validate Data can now fit linear mixed model verify simulated fixed effects, random effects, induced correlation structure behaving intended: estimated treatment--time interaction, residual variation, random-effects covariance close data-generating values. title: Solve exponential rate parameters from target observed event probabilities — rate_from_prob
text: Assume single event time \(T \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_e)\) independent censoring time \(C \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_c)\). probability observing event $$ P(T < C) = \frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_e + \lambda_c}. $$ Given \(\lambda_e\) target probability \(p\), function solves censoring rate \(\lambda_c\): $$ \lambda_c = \frac{\lambda_e}{p} - \lambda_e. $$ mode, returned value required independent censoring rate.

title: Solve exponential rate parameters from target observed event probabilities — rate_from_prob
text: Assume single event time \(T \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_e)\) fixed administrative censoring time \(> 0\). probability observing event time \(\) $$ P(T \le ) = 1 - e^{-\lambda_e }. $$ Given \(\) target probability \(p\), function solves event rate \(\lambda_e\): $$ \lambda_e = -\frac{\log(1 - p)}{}. $$ mode, returned value required event rate.
